questions.q: How does the editorial distinguish discussion from debate?
options: Debate is for scholars; discussion is for ordinary people
Not quite. The article says: Debate aims at proving superiority; discussion aims at mutual learning.
Debate ends in agreement; discussion does not
Not quite. The article says: Debate aims at proving superiority; discussion aims at mutual learning.
Debate is spoken; discussion is written
Not quite. The article says: Debate aims at proving superiority; discussion aims at mutual learning.
Debate aims at proving superiority; discussion aims at mutual learning
Yes. Differences become a chance to learn.
questions.rationale: “The purpose of debate is to establish superiority… The purpose of discussion—on the other hand—is mutual learning; taking something and giving something.”

questions.q: A reader objected that the author had used examples from secular people. Which saying of the Prophet settled the matter?
options: The best of you are those of best character
Not quite. The article says: Wisdom is the lost property of a believer; wherever he finds it, he should take it.
Seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave
Not quite. The article says: Wisdom is the lost property of a believer; wherever he finds it, he should take it.
Wisdom is the lost property of a believer; wherever he finds it, he should take it
Well done. The man replied that his knowledge had increased.
Actions are judged by intentions
Not quite. The article says: Wisdom is the lost property of a believer; wherever he finds it, he should take it.
questions.rationale: The author quoted: “Wisdom is the lost property of a believer; wherever he finds it, he should take it as his own.”

questions.q: Why does the article say that whatever a person earns is “a direct favour from God”?
options: Because human effort plays no part in earning
Not quite. The article says: Both his abilities and a world made to serve him are given by God.
Both his abilities and a world made to serve him are given by God
Right. So wealth should be spent as God wishes.
Because earning is itself an act of worship
Not quite. The article says: Both his abilities and a world made to serve him are given by God.
Because wealth comes only to those who pray for it
Not quite. The article says: Both his abilities and a world made to serve him are given by God.
questions.rationale: “If the world and that which it contains had not been placed at man’s disposal, his physical and mental capabilities alone would never have enabled him to derive any benefit.”

questions.q: The article mentions Akbar’s Deen-e-Ilahi and Dr Bhagwan Das’s encyclopaedia. What do these examples show?
options: Religious unity needs the power of the state
Not quite. The article says: Attempts to declare all religions one and the same have not succeeded.
India has no tradition of tolerance
Not quite. The article says: Attempts to declare all religions one and the same have not succeeded.
Rulers and scholars have always opposed religion
Not quite. The article says: Attempts to declare all religions one and the same have not succeeded.
Attempts to declare all religions one and the same have not succeeded
Correct. The workable formula is “Follow one and respect all.”
questions.rationale: The article holds that treating all religions as equally true is “unnatural as well as irrational,” and points to the Quran: “For you, your religion; for me, mine.”

questions.q: According to the article, why does suffering caused by human evil exist in the world?
options: Man is being tested, which requires freedom, and some misuse it
Yes. Without freedom, good deeds would earn no credit.
God does not intervene in human affairs
Not quite. The article says: Man is being tested, which requires freedom, and some misuse it.
Everything in history is fixed in advance
Not quite. The article says: Man is being tested, which requires freedom, and some misuse it.
Suffering is an illusion
Not quite. The article says: Man is being tested, which requires freedom, and some misuse it.
questions.rationale: “Man can be granted the credit for a good deed only on the condition that, despite having the opportunity to indulge in bad deeds, he chooses of his own free will to act virtuously.”

questions.q: Elias Howe found in a dream where the eye of the sewing-machine needle should go. What does the article say the dream shows?
options: That he should have rested more
Not quite. The article says: That he was so absorbed in his work that it filled even his subconscious mind.
That dreams foretell the future
Not quite. The article says: That he was so absorbed in his work that it filled even his subconscious mind.
That he was so absorbed in his work that it filled even his subconscious mind
Exactly. Success follows complete involvement.
That great inventions come by luck
Not quite. The article says: That he was so absorbed in his work that it filled even his subconscious mind.
questions.rationale: “What is a dream? It is the result of complete involvement… One achieves success in one’s aim only after complete involvement.”

questions.q: Why does the article call secularism “a great blessing for religion”?
options: It has made religion part of the government
Not quite. The article says: As a policy of non-interference, it ended persecution and left religious people free to work.
It has replaced religion with science
Not quite. The article says: As a policy of non-interference, it ended persecution and left religious people free to work.
As a policy of non-interference, it ended persecution and left religious people free to work
Well read. The two are called complementary.
It has shown all religions to be the same
Not quite. The article says: As a policy of non-interference, it ended persecution and left religious people free to work.
questions.rationale: “Secularism is a policy of non-interference in religious matters… There is no clash between religion and secularism.”

questions.q: What does the article mean by saying that man lives in “a fool’s paradise of his own making”?
options: He trusts other people too easily
Not quite. The article says: He measures himself by his own standards and worldly success, forgetting the reckoning before God.
He measures himself by his own standards and worldly success, forgetting the reckoning before God
Yes. Only God’s standard will count.
He believes too readily in life after death
Not quite. The article says: He measures himself by his own standards and worldly success, forgetting the reckoning before God.
He spends too much time in worship
Not quite. The article says: He measures himself by his own standards and worldly success, forgetting the reckoning before God.
questions.rationale: “People have set up their own standards about what is right and what is wrong… How shocked they will be when they learn that only those were in the right, who lived up to the standard set by God!”

questions.q: Why is charity (sadqa fitr) to be given well before the Eid prayer?
options: So that the amount is known in advance
Not quite. The article says: So that the poor can also take part in the celebration.
So that mosques can be decorated
Not quite. The article says: So that the poor can also take part in the celebration.
So that the giver’s fast is counted
Not quite. The article says: So that the poor can also take part in the celebration.
So that the poor can also take part in the celebration
Correct. Real happiness lies in sharing.
questions.rationale: “Alms should be given well before the Eid day so that the poor may take part in the celebrations as well.”

questions.q: In the article’s reading, what do fasting and the breaking of the fast each represent?
options: Fasting stands for this life of test and restraint; the breaking of the fast and Eid for the Hereafter
Right. Eid gives “a faint taste” of what is to come.
Both stand for the hardships of this world
Not quite. The article says: Fasting stands for this life of test and restraint; the breaking of the fast and Eid for the Hereafter.
Fasting stands for the Hereafter; feasting for this world
Not quite. The article says: Fasting stands for this life of test and restraint; the breaking of the fast and Eid for the Hereafter.
Fasting stands for the body; feasting for the soul
Not quite. The article says: Fasting stands for this life of test and restraint; the breaking of the fast and Eid for the Hereafter.
questions.rationale: “Fasting is a semblance of this test… In contrast to fasting, Iftar (breaking the fast), presents a semblance of life Hereafter.”
